meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The future ain't what it used to be'?
meta.ogDescription: Berra popularised it, but didn't coin it: the saying is documented in English in 1937 by Laura Riding and Robert Graves.

answer.label: Not originated by Yogi Berra — the line dates to 1937
answer.authorDates: Riding 1901–1991 · Graves 1895–1985 · poets and co-editors of the journal Epilogue
answer.sourceLine: Quote Investigator’s earliest evidence is a 1937 piece by Laura Riding and Robert Graves in their journal Epilogue: “the future is not what it used to be” — the first instance located in English, with Paul Valéry writing a French version the same year. The colloquial “ain’t” wording is first documented in 1973, credited to an English professor; Yogi Berra claimed and popularised it later, and Wikiquote files it under his Misattributed section.

source.excerpt: The human mind has reached the end of temporal progress: the future is not what it used to be.
trail: 1937 — the first English instance. Laura Riding and Robert Graves write “the future is not what it used to be” in their journal Epilogue, the earliest evidence located by Quote Investigator ↗.

1937 / 1948 — Valéry in French, then in English. “Notre Destin et Les Lettres” carries the same idea; the essay appears in English as “Our Destiny and Literature” in Reflections on the World Today, translated by Francis Scarfe and published by Pantheon in 1948 — Internet Archive ↗.
1973 — the “ain’t” appears. A Boston Globe article credits the colloquial form to English professor Gary Goshgarian, per Quote Investigator ↗.
1998 — Berra claims it. The Yogi Book presents the saying as his, with no date given and a 1974 photograph alongside; Wikiquote nonetheless lists it among his misattributed lines ↗.
source.excerptNote: As transcribed by Quote Investigator from the 1937 Epilogue piece. Note the wording: no “ain’t” — that colloquial form is not documented until 1973.

source.rightsNote: No public-domain claim is made here. The exact “ain’t” wording has no identified authored source — its earliest documented appearance is a 1973 newspaper article — and every work in the trail was first published after 1930: the 1937 Epilogue piece by Riding and Graves, Valéry’s 1937 essay, the 1948 Scarfe translation and Berra’s own book all remain within copyright terms in the United States.

author.name: Laura Riding & Robert Graves
author.heading: Who actually wrote it first
author.metaLine: Riding 1901–1991 · Graves 1895–1985 · poets, critics and co-editors of Epilogue
author.bio: Laura Riding (1901–1991) was an American poet, critic and novelist; Robert Graves (1895–1985) was the English poet, novelist and critic behind Goodbye to All That and I, Claudius. After meeting in the mid-1920s the pair moved to Deià, Mallorca, where they ran the Seizin Press and founded and edited the critical magazine Epilogue, published between 1935 and 1938. It is in a 1937 Epilogue piece, “From a Private Correspondence on Reality,” that Quote Investigator finds the earliest English instance of the saying that would later travel the world in Yogi Berra’s voice.

cite.sourceCitation: Laura Riding and Robert Graves, "From a Private Correspondence on Reality," Epilogue (1937), as documented in "Quote Origin: The Future Is Not What It Used To Be," Quote Investigator, December 6, 2012, https://quoteinvestigator.com/2012/12/06/future-not-used/. Compare Paul Valéry, "Our Destiny and Literature," in Reflections on the World Today, trans. Francis Scarfe (New York: Pantheon, 1948).

misattribution.heading: Who gets the credit, and why
misattribution.intro: This is a textbook quote-magnet case: an old bit of wordplay that drifted onto a famous, funny name and stuck there.

items.why: Berra claimed the expression in his 1998 volume The Yogi Book, without giving a date; the entry was accompanied by a 1974 photograph, per Quote Investigator ↗. The saying was already in print decades earlier, and Wikiquote files it under Misattributed on his quote page ↗.

Valéry wrote in 1937, in the essay “Notre Destin et Les Lettres,” “L’avenir est comme le reste: il n’est plus ce qu’il était,” rendered in English in 1948 as “The future, like everything else, is no longer quite what it used to be” — a real source for the thought, but not for the snappy English wording, per Quote Investigator ↗.

items.tag: Earliest documented use of this form
items.why: Quote Investigator’s earliest citation using “ain’t” is a 1973 Boston Globe article, where the line is ascribed to English professor Gary Goshgarian — see the chronology ↗. That is an attestation, not proof of coinage.

misattribution.truthLine: Best evidence: the saying appears in English in 1937 with Laura Riding and Robert Graves, and in French the same year with Paul Valéry; the “ain’t” form is first documented in 1973 and Yogi Berra made it famous — Quote Investigator ↗.

context.heading: Why this one sticks to Yogi
lead: Yogi Berra is one of the great quote magnets: a beloved, funny, plain-spoken man whose real verbal tics made almost any paradox sound like his. He knew it himself — he titled his own collection The Yogi Book: I Really Didn’t Say Everything I Said.

This line fits the mould perfectly, but the joke was already in print in 1937, in a journal edited by two very literary poets, and again the same year in French from Paul Valéry. What Berra did was give it the shrug and the “ain’t” — and once a saying is in his voice, it tends to stay there.
detailsBody: Quote Investigator’s chronology shows the idea circulating steadily for decades before Berra was ever attached to it: a 1959 Milwaukee Sentinel instance with no attribution, a 1962 Chicago Tribune notice of a talk titled “The Future Is Not What it Used to Be,” and a 1975 Reader’s Digest dictionary crediting Valéry.
The specifically colloquial form — with “ain’t” — appears in a 1973 Boston Globe article, where it is credited to English professor Gary Goshgarian, per Quote Investigator.
context.pull: He popularised it. He didn’t coin it.
